title: How Employees’ Emotional Labor Promotes Perceived Service Quality: A Dual-Pathway Model
content: Despite service firms realizing that frontline employees’ emotional labor is important for fostering perceived service quality and improving sustainable competitiveness, the underlying theoretical mechanisms for this phenomenon remain unclear. Drawing on the emotions as social information (EASI) model, we proposed that employees’ emotional labor affects customer perceived service quality through both the emotional contagion pathway and the inferential pathway. Furthermore, the relative impact of either pathway depends on customer involvement. Using dyadic data from frontline employees and customers in banking industry, the results indicated that: employees’ emotional labor exerts significant influence on perceived service quality. Different from surface acting whose effect on service quality is only mediated by customer positive affect (through emotional contagion pathway), deep acting’s effects on service quality are mediated both by customer positive affect (through emotional contagion pathway) and customer participation (through emotional inferential pathway). Furthermore, customer involvement moderates the positive link of deep acting and customer participation, and the negative link of surface acting and customer positive affect.
